books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Photograph, Assembly line at the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park plant, 1913

stimulus.text: The photograph shows a row of Model T chassis — frames with wheels, engines, and steering wheels, but no bodies — moving along a conveyor line inside a large factory hall at Ford's Highland Park plant in 1913. Overhead belts and wheels drive the line. No workers are visible in this view.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph, Assembly line at the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park plant, 1913, Library of Congress LCCN2011661021, public domain.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Library of Congress photograph, 1913, public domain
stem: The assembly line changed factory work most directly by

options.text: giving each worker control of a whole car
options.misconception: Background from the books: the line took whole-car building away from skilled workers, so each worker did less, not more.

options.text: splitting car building into small repeated tasks
ending the use of machines in factories
options.misconception: Machines were central to the line. The belts and conveyors are visible in the photo.

options.text: paying workers only when cars were sold
options.misconception: Ford paid workers by the day, not only when cars sold. The five-dollar day was a daily wage.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the line took whole-car building away from skilled workers, so each worker did less, not more.
rationales.B: Each worker did one small task as the chassis moved past. That split the work into small repeated steps, which was the point of the line.
rationales.C: Machines were central to the line. The belts and conveyors are visible in the photo.
rationales.D: Ford paid workers by the day, not only when cars sold. The five-dollar day was a daily wage.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the old way: a skilled worker built much of a car himself.
2. Look at the photo: the chassis moves, and each station adds one part.
3. Name the change: the job is split into small steps, so each worker repeats one task.
Remember: when a new method divides work, ask what each worker still does and what each worker loses.
